about: The character hints in the book and the workpapers and tools they point to (bookpals11). Read by tools/book/hints.py. Workpapers are pages you fill in; tools are interactive helpers on the site. Which list an item is shown in comes from its kind in /assets/js/tools-registry.js (the single source of truth; the calculators and the practice playground are tools); the two lists here are only the fallback for items the registry doesn't list. Keep them separate: a hint names at most one of each, on its own line. 'print' is the short address printed on paper (a page that exists, without .html).
kinds_about: Links the registry does not list as written, with their kind: the Individual package is every workpaper of the self path in one PDF; /quick-checks.html is My weather today (registry: #today); /perspective-shifter.html now opens Rewind the talk’s “See their side” step; /communication-style-quiz.html is the quiz’s own page.

hints.text: Sugarfoot’s tip: go slowly in this part. It’s all about you, and you’re worth the time. A one-minute check on how you are today is a gentle way in.
Tidbit wants you to know: this part comes with workpapers to fill in, together or on your own. Ooh, start with the one-week log!
If a question pops up while you read, ask me. Nothing you type leaves your device.
Tidbit wants you to know: the rules from home aren’t good or bad, they’re just yours to have a good sniff at. A fun first look is how you like to talk.
When an old rule jumps in before you’ve had a chance to think, you don’t have to argue with it. Write it down, and look at it again on a calm day.

hints.after_heading: Why a lens isn’t a fault
hints.text: A lens is just the angle you learned to look from. Before you change anything, it helps to see it: this tool walks you back from a feeling to the rule underneath it.
Sugarfoot’s tip: write your rulebook slowly, one line at a time. Nobody has to see it. When you’re ready to share a rule you’ve chosen, a one-page card can say it for you.

Old rules often show up first in small things at home, like who notices the empty fridge. A one-week log makes those habits easy to see, without blaming anyone. Take it from a raindrop: small drops are how a puddle starts.
Your wiring stays the same from day to day. Your weather doesn’t. A one-minute check in the morning helps you tell the two apart.
Sugarfoot’s tip: make your calm-down plan on a slow, sunny day, maybe with a cup of tea. It’s much easier than making it in the middle of a storm.

hints.after_heading: Why it helps to describe your wiring
hints.text: Describing your wiring is a kindness to the people around you: it saves them guessing. The one-page card puts it in your own words, ready to share or to keep.

hints.after_heading: Why a reading on ordinary days helps
hints.text: Tidbit wants you to know: checking your weather on a boring day totally counts! Ordinary days are how you find out what normal looks like for you.

hints.after_heading: Why you plan it while calm
hints.text: A plan written while you’re calm is a note from your steadier self. The Calm-Down Kit gives it a shape: what helps, what doesn’t, and one sentence to say when you need a pause.
Tidbit wants you to know: tiny steps count, even the wobbly ones! If you like a game, there’s one where each small kind act moves the ball up the field.
Your monthly look is the solo version of the monthly look-back for people who share a home. Borrow its two questions if you like: what kept slipping, and what would have made it easier?

hints.after_heading: Why kindness works better than a stick
hints.text: Sugarfoot’s tip: when a step slips, talk to yourself the way you’d talk to a friend who tried. Then pick the smallest next step. If the kind words won’t come, Professor Puddles is good at finding them.
The easiest way to see unseen work is to write it down for one ordinary week. Each of you logs only your own jobs, and the thinking counts too.
Tidbit wants you to know: counting jobs isn’t keeping score. It’s more like a treasure hunt for the work nobody noticed! The quick split check is a good first sniff.

hints.after_heading: Handing over a whole job, thinking included
hints.text: Sugarfoot’s tip: when you hand over a job, hand over the whole of it, the remembering too. Giving every job one owner means nobody has to carry it in their head “just in case”.

On the way through, Tidbit, Sugarfoot and I pop up with small hints. A workpaper is a page you fill in; a tool is a helper you use on the site. This chapter’s workpaper is the one-week log, and its quick tool is the split check.
Tidbit’s tip: short on time? The two-minute snapshot is a speedy first look before a whole week of logging. Zoom!
Ooh, Tidbit loves this one: compare your daily rhythms and see whose engine runs fast in the morning and whose at night. Different speeds aren’t wrong, just different!
When you go back in, one clear sentence beats a speech. This workpaper helps you shape it before you say it.
Pace is one of the quiet causes of static. This workpaper lets each of you write down your own pace, then compare notes without blame.

Sugarfoot’s tip: if a talk has already gone wrong, that’s all right. Take a slow breath first, then try Rewind the talk together.
The smallest habit in this chapter often does the most: three short questions, once a day. The daily check-in keeps them in one place.
Sugarfoot’s tip: one bad evening isn’t the whole story. Give it a month, then run the check together, slowly, with a snack.
A job without a name tends to land on whoever notices first. Write one owner next to each job, and the guessing stops.
The check only works if the hidden jobs are counted too. A one-week log, with the planning and remembering written in, gives you honest numbers to start from.
Tidbit wants you to know: the stress input is just five quick questions about how full your tank is. No wrong answers, promise!
The score judges the setup, never a person. Let the calculator do the sums, and save your energy for the talk afterwards. Even a professor would rather not do long division at the kitchen table.
Before a hard talk, check how full your own tank is. Five quick questions, about two minutes, and you’ll know whether now is the time.
Tidbit’s tip: say your number out loud, like “I’m a seven today.” It’s quick, and nobody has to guess!
Before a hard talk, check how full your own tank is. Five quick questions, about two minutes, and you’ll know whether now is the time.
Sugarfoot’s tip: a full tank means “later”, not “never”. If you’re both upset right now, take five minutes to settle, then pick a time to come back.
When two angles both feel true, try writing out the other person’s side in their words. Rewind the talk has a “See their side” step for exactly that.
Tidbit wants you to know: children love it when their favourite things make the trip too! A handoff-bag checklist keeps track between two homes.
Sugarfoot’s tip: covering for someone is kind. Say it out loud, gently, and ask for what you’d like next time, so it doesn’t turn into quiet resentment.
When a comment stings, give it a minute to land before you answer. This workpaper is a short check for your reply.
Whichever kind of fair you choose, write the owners down. Keep the list short: one name per job, and a backup for the busy weeks.
Tidbit wants you to know: “I’ll take the bins this week, can you take them next week?” is a great sentence. Turning a grumble into a request is a whole tool!
Before you reply to a comment that stung, give it a minute to land. The workpaper is a short check for your reply, and the Chat analyzer can help you read a message that has just come in.
Sugarfoot’s tip: money talks go better on a slow evening, not a rushed morning. It can help to count the hours and the money together first.
The look-back has its own workpaper: a month of notes, one list, and an ✗ for each week a job slipped. It makes a pattern easy to see.
Tidbit wants you to know: a look-back can start with a high five. Name one thing that went well first! The weekly card has a nice way to begin.

hints.after_heading: Three ways to read the book
hints.text: As you read, Tidbit, Sugarfoot and I pop up with small hints. A workpaper is a page you fill in; a tool is a helper you use on the site. If you’re short on time, start here.

hints.after_heading: Part One, Now: what settles you
hints.text: Sugarfoot’s tip: the best time to plan for a stormy moment is a calm one. Make your kit today, while things are quiet.

hints.after_heading: Chapter II: is the split working?
hints.text: Tidbit wants you to know: the quick split check takes a few minutes and shows who does what at a glance. Ready, steady, sniff!

hints.after_heading: Chapter IV: let a comment land before you react
hints.text: A message that stung often reads differently an hour later. The Chat analyzer can help you read it calmly before you reply.

hints.after_heading: Part One, Now: your wiring, your weather and your words
hints.text: Tidbit’s tip: quick talker or slow thinker? There’s a fun quiz to find out, and it’s even more fun to compare answers.
Sugarfoot’s tip: sharing a room goes more smoothly with a few things agreed early, like quiet hours and guests. Write them down together.
